summary: EU, US, UK and many other passports enter Serbia visa-free for 90 days, and Russia, China, Belarus, the UAE and Bahrain enter visa-free too. Holders of a valid Schengen, EU, UK or US visa or residence permit can also enter without a Serbian visa. Remaining nationalities apply for a visa at a Serbian embassy or online.

conditionalWaivers.text: Holders of a valid Schengen, EU member state, UK or US visa — or a residence permit issued by a Schengen country, an EU member state or the US — can enter Serbia visa-free for up to 90 days in a six-month period, regardless of nationality. The stay cannot exceed the validity of the visa or residence permit you are traveling on, and the rule does not cover emergency travel documents or travel documents issued under international conventions.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia — Visa Requirements
Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia — Visa Requirements
Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia — Visa Requirements

passportValidity.text: Serbia requires a travel document valid at least 90 days after the intended date of departure for visa applications; the UK FCDO gives the same 90-day rule for visa-free visitors. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs says citizens of EU countries such as Germany and of neighbouring Balkan states such as Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Montenegro and Albania can also travel with an ID card.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia — Visa Requirements

travelInsurance.text: Visa applicants must hold adequate, valid travel medical insurance. For all visitors the Foreign Ministry recommends health insurance for the whole stay covering at least EUR 20,000 of medical costs, and border police may ask for proof of it.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia — Visa requirements (travel to Serbia)

onwardTicket.text: No official source we could read requires an onward ticket. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs says border authorities may ask to see a return flight ticket and a paid hotel booking or proof of a private address, among other documents.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia — General Entry Requirements

proofOfFunds.text: Foreigners must be able to show sufficient funds for their stay: EUR 50 per day, in cash or as a bank statement. Border police may refuse entry to anyone who cannot.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia — General Entry Requirements

declarations.name: Address registration (white card)
declarations.text: The UK FCDO says you must register with the local police where you are staying within 24 hours of arrival, that hotels register you automatically, and that if you do not register you could be fined, arrested and taken to court. Canada says registration is normally arranged by your hotel or host.

source.name: UK FCDO — Serbia travel advice (entry requirements)

currencyLimits.text: Cash of more than €10,000 (or equivalent) must be declared on entry and exit; undeclared amounts can be confiscated.

source.name: Customs Administration of Serbia — Useful information for passengers

notes: The UK Foreign Office says you must declare personal items of value you are carrying, such as jewellery, cameras and computers; they are exempt from customs duties. Canada adds that you must take them with you when you leave.
The UK Foreign Office says that if you bring Serbian dinars into the country you must show the receipt from the bank where you bought them, and advises exchanging unwanted dinars before you leave.

payments.text: No official source we could read describes card acceptance in Serbia. Canada's travel advice says euros are not legal tender but all banks and exchange offices readily convert them; the UK Foreign Office says to change money only at banks or official exchange offices, never with street dealers.

safety.text: The UK FCDO says mass gatherings and demonstrations are taking place in Belgrade and other towns and some have turned violent, that pickpockets work in tourist areas, airports and on public transport, and that violent incidents are common around Red Star–Partizan derby matches. Canada advises normal security precautions, and a high degree of caution within 10 km of the border with Kosovo.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Serbia travel advice

idp.text: Serbia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

driving.text: Serbia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Serbia yet.

tips.text: The UK FCDO says that to travel from Kosovo to Serbia you need a Serbian entry stamp from Belgrade, Niš or Kraljevo airport or from a land crossing with a neighbouring country, and that without one you are likely to be refused entry. Canada says to transit via a third country instead.

The UK Foreign Office says it knows of isolated incidents where Serbian authorities have cancelled Kosovo stamps in foreign nationals' passports or refused entry to people with Republic of Kosovo stamps.

You must register with the local police within 24 hours of arrival. Canada says registration is normally arranged by your hotel or host, and that failure to register can result in fines and difficulties when departing.

The UK Foreign Office says to change money only through banks or official exchange offices and not to use street dealers. British banks do not normally exchange dinars, so change unwanted dinars before you leave.
Serbia is not part of the Schengen Area, so days spent here do not count against the 90/180 Schengen allowance.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Serbia?
faq.answer: Most visitors do not. Citizens of the EU, US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and most of Europe and the Americas enter visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period, and Serbia also waives visas for Russia, China, Belarus, the UAE and Bahrain (30–90 days). Nationalities outside the waiver lists apply at a Serbian embassy or consulate, or online.

faq.question: Can I enter Serbia from Kosovo?
faq.answer: Only with a Serbian entry stamp. The UK FCDO says Serbia does not consider the crossing points with Kosovo to be official international border crossings, so to travel from Kosovo to Serbia you need a Serbian entry stamp from Belgrade, Niš or Kraljevo airport or from a land crossing with a neighbouring country; without one you are likely to be refused entry.

faq.question: How long can Russian citizens stay in Serbia?
faq.answer: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs says Russian holders of ordinary passports need no visa for visits of up to 30 days.

faq.question: Can EU citizens enter Serbia with just an ID card?
faq.answer: Yes. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs says citizens of EU countries such as Germany, and of neighbouring states such as Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Montenegro and Albania, can travel to Serbia with an ID card.

faq.question: Is Serbia in the EU or Schengen?
faq.answer: No — Serbia belongs to neither the EU nor Schengen. Time spent in Serbia does not count against your 90/180-day Schengen allowance. The UK FCDO says to make sure border guards stamp your passport when you enter.

faq.question: Do I have to register with the police in Serbia?
faq.answer: Yes, within 24 hours of arrival. The UK FCDO says hotels register you automatically and that failing to register can bring a fine, arrest and a court appearance; Canada says registration is normally arranged by your hotel or host.
